lessons.briefing: Every disease outbreak follows predictable rules governed by the relationship between a pathogen, a susceptible host, and the environment. Understanding the epidemiological triangle, basic reproduction number (R0), herd immunity thresholds, and transmission routes is the foundation for all community disease prevention and outbreak control work.
lessons.contentMd:
## The Epidemiological Triangle

Every infectious disease requires three elements to sustain transmission:

| Element | Definition | Example levers |
|---|---|---|
| Agent | The pathogen (virus, bacterium, parasite, prion) | Antibiotic/antiviral treatment |
| Host | The susceptible person or animal | Vaccination, nutrition, immune status |
| Environment | The physical/social conditions enabling contact | Sanitation, housing, vector control |

Removing or weakening **any one** side of the triangle breaks transmission.

## Transmission Routes

| Route | Mechanism | Typical pathogens |
|---|---|---|
| Direct contact | Skin-to-skin, mucous membrane | Scabies, STIs, ringworm |
| Droplet | Particles > 5 microns, range < 1 m | Influenza, COVID-19, meningococcal |
| Airborne | Particles < 5 microns (aerosols), long range | TB, measles, chickenpox |
| Faecal-oral | Contaminated water or food | Cholera, typhoid, hepatitis A |
| Vector-borne | Arthropod bite transmits pathogen | Malaria (Anopheles), dengue (Aedes) |
| Fomite | Contaminated surface, object | Norovirus, RSV, C. difficile |

Understanding route is critical: a droplet disease like influenza is controlled
by masks and spacing; an airborne disease like TB requires negative-pressure
ventilation.

## Basic Reproduction Number (R0)

R0 = average number of secondary cases one infectious person generates in a
fully susceptible population.

| Disease | R0 | Control difficulty |
|---|---|---|
| Measles | 12-18 | Very high |
| Pertussis (whooping cough) | 12-17 | Very high |
| Chickenpox | 10-12 | High |
| COVID-19 (original) | 2-4 | Moderate |
| Influenza (seasonal) | 1.2-1.4 | Low |
| Ebola | 1.5-2.5 | Moderate (if no isolation) |
| Cholera | 2-6 | Moderate |

When R_eff (effective R0 after interventions) drops below 1.0, the outbreak
collapses. Every intervention — vaccination, isolation, hygiene — reduces R_eff.

## Herd Immunity Threshold

The proportion of the population that must be immune to prevent sustained
transmission:

HIT = 1 - (1 / R0)

| Disease | R0 | HIT required |
|---|---|---|
| Measles | 15 | 93% |
| Polio | 6 | 83% |
| COVID-19 (Delta) | 5-6 | 80-83% |
| Influenza | 1.3 | 23% |

This is why measles outbreaks reappear in communities where vaccination
coverage drops even slightly below 93% — there is almost no margin.

## Attack Rate & Case Fatality Rate

**Attack Rate (AR)**: proportion of exposed people who develop disease.

AR = (cases / exposed population) x 100%

**Case Fatality Rate (CFR)**: proportion of confirmed cases who die.

CFR = (deaths / confirmed cases) x 100%

| Disease | Typical CFR (untreated) | CFR with treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Cholera | 25-50% | < 1% |
| Malaria (severe) | 20-30% | 10-15% |
| Meningococcal disease | 50% | 5-10% |
| Measles (malnourished children) | 10-30% | 1-5% |

These dramatic CFR reductions show the life-saving value of early treatment.

## The Disease Iceberg

Most infectious diseases have a large proportion of asymptomatic or mild cases
below the "waterline" — invisible to passive surveillance:

- Polio: 1 paralytic case per 200 infected (0.5% visible)
- COVID-19: 30-80% asymptomatic depending on variant
- Typhoid: ~10% symptomatic
- Cholera: ~75% asymptomatic (El Tor biotype)

Implications: case counts always underestimate true infection burden;
asymptomatic carriers sustain transmission silently.

exercises.explanation:
HIT = 1 - (1/15) = 1 - 0.067 = 0.933 = 93.3%. At 88% coverage, 12% are susceptible — above the 6.7% threshold needed to sustain transmission. An outbreak is possible.

Why the other options are wrong: The 80% figure applies to diseases with R0 of 5-6. Measles R0 of 15 requires 93% coverage, not 80%. 50% corresponds to diseases with R0 = 2. For measles R0 = 15, even 90% coverage leaves enough susceptibles to sustain spread. Nutrition affects severity (CFR) but not whether measles spreads. Coverage against a threshold is the transmission control mechanism.

options.text: No — the herd immunity threshold for measles is 93%, so at 88% coverage an outbreak can still spread
Yes — 88% coverage is well above the 80% threshold for most diseases
Yes — once coverage exceeds 50% the outbreak will collapse
It depends on nutrition status, not vaccination coverage

exercises.prompt: Measles has an R0 of approximately 15. A community of 1,000 children has 88% vaccination coverage. Is this sufficient to prevent an outbreak?

exercises.explanation: Cholera: HIT = 1 - (1/4) = 0.75 = 75%. Influenza: HIT = 1 - (1/1.3) = 1 - 0.769 = 0.231 = 23%. The low influenza HIT explains why annual flu campaigns with even moderate uptake can significantly reduce transmission.
exercises.prompt: The herd immunity threshold formula is HIT = 1 - (1 / R0). For cholera with R0 = 4, the HIT is ___%. For seasonal influenza with R0 = 1.3, the HIT is approximately ___%.

exercises.explanation: Matching the intervention to the route is the first step in outbreak control. Wrong interventions waste resources without breaking transmission.

right.text: Negative-pressure isolation rooms and N95 respirators
Safe water, sanitation, and handwashing (WASH)
Insecticide-treated bed nets and indoor residual spraying
Surgical masks, 1 m physical distancing

exercises.prompt: Match each transmission route to its primary control intervention.

exercises.explanation:
AR = 480/3200 x 100 = 15%. CFR = 12/480 x 100 = 2.5%. A CFR of 2.5% indicates some access to ORT treatment (untreated cholera CFR is 25-50%).

Why the other options are wrong: These are reversed. AR uses the exposed population (3,200) as denominator; CFR uses confirmed cases (480) as denominator. AR is correct. CFR is not deaths/exposed but deaths/confirmed cases: 12/480 = 2.5%, not 0.37%. 0.37% would be deaths/exposed (12/3200). AR is cases/exposed = 480/3200 = 15%.
exercises.prompt: During a cholera outbreak, 3,200 people drank water from a contaminated river. 480 developed cholera. 12 of those died. What are the attack rate and case fatality rate?

exercises.explanation: Polio: 1 paralytic per 200 infected = iceberg ratio of 200. COVID-19: 600 symptomatic = 30% of total; total = 600/0.30 = 2,000 true infections. This undercounting has major implications for surveillance — reported cases are always a fraction of true burden.
exercises.prompt: For every 1 paralytic polio case seen, approximately ___ people are actually infected (the disease iceberg). During a COVID-19 wave where 30% of infections are symptomatic, if a clinic records 600 symptomatic cases, the estimated true infection count is ___.

lessons.outline: The epidemiological triangle (agent, host, environment); transmission routes (direct contact, droplet, airborne, faecal-oral, vector-borne, fomite); R0 and R_eff — what they mean for outbreak dynamics; herd immunity threshold formula; attack rate and case fatality rate; incubation period vs infectious period; the disease iceberg (symptomatic vs asymptomatic).

lessons.briefing: Diarrhoeal disease kills approximately 1.6 million people per year globally — the vast majority are children under 5 in low-income settings. Oral rehydration therapy (ORT), a simple solution of sugar, salt, and water, can reduce cholera CFR from 50% to under 1%. Every community health worker must be able to prepare ORT from local materials, assess dehydration severity, and know when to escalate to intravenous fluids.
lessons.contentMd:
## Pathophysiology of Secretory Diarrhoea

In cholera, the CT (cholera toxin) activates intestinal cAMP, forcing massive
chloride secretion into the gut lumen. Water follows osmotically, producing
"rice-water stools" at up to 1 litre per hour. The patient loses:

- Sodium (Na+): 90-140 mmol/L in stool
- Potassium (K+): 20-30 mmol/L
- Bicarbonate (HCO3-): 30-50 mmol/L
- Water: up to 20 L/day in severe cases

Replacing these electrolytes and water is the entire treatment. There is no
anti-toxin. ORT works by using the sodium-glucose co-transporter (SGLT1)
in the gut wall — glucose carries sodium across even when the secretory
pump is maximally activated.

## WHO Dehydration Assessment

Assess three clinical signs:

| Sign | No dehydration | Some dehydration (2 signs = confirm) | Severe dehydration (2 signs = confirm) |
|---|---|---|---|
| General appearance | Well, alert | Restless, irritable | Lethargic or unconscious |
| Eyes | Normal | Sunken | Very sunken, dry |
| Mouth/tongue | Moist | Dry | Very dry |
| Skin pinch | Returns immediately | Returns slowly (< 2s) | Returns very slowly (> 2s) |
| Thirst | Not thirsty | Thirsty, drinks eagerly | Unable to drink |

If **2 or more signs** in the severe column → IV fluids + urgent referral.

## WHO ORS Formulation (per 1 litre water)

| Ingredient | Amount |
|---|---|
| Sodium chloride (table salt) | 3.5 g (or 0.6 teaspoon) |
| Trisodium citrate | 2.9 g (or use 2.5 g sodium bicarbonate) |
| Potassium chloride | 1.5 g |
| Glucose (anhydrous) | 20.0 g |

If commercial ORS sachet unavailable — **home-made ORT** (temporary substitute):

- 1 litre clean water (boiled and cooled)
- 6 level teaspoons of sugar (30 g)
- 0.5 teaspoon of salt (2.5 g)

Home-made ORT contains no potassium or bicarbonate — adequate for mild/moderate
cases but not for severe cholera requiring full electrolyte replacement.

## ORT Administration — WHO Treatment Plans

### Plan A (No dehydration — home treatment)
- Give ORS after every loose stool
- Children under 2: 50-100 mL per stool
- Children 2-10: 100-200 mL per stool
- Adults/children over 10: as much as desired
- Continue normal feeding

### Plan B (Some dehydration — clinic/facility)
- Give 75 mL/kg of ORS over 4 hours
- Example: 20 kg child = 1,500 mL over 4 hours = 375 mL/hour
- Re-assess after 4 hours; upgrade to Plan C if deteriorating

### Plan C (Severe dehydration — IV fluids essential)
- Adults and children over 5: Ringer's Lactate 100 mL/kg IV over 3 hours
- Children under 5: RL 100 mL/kg IV over 6 hours (30 mL/kg in first 30 min)
- If IV not immediately available: nasogastric ORS at 20 mL/kg/hour
- Seek hospital transfer urgently

## Zinc Supplementation

WHO recommends zinc given alongside ORT for all children under 5 with diarrhoea:

- Under 6 months: 10 mg elemental zinc per day for 10-14 days
- 6 months to 5 years: 20 mg per day for 10-14 days

Evidence: zinc reduces duration of diarrhoea episode by 25%, severity by 30%,
and probability of subsequent episode in 2-3 months by 50% (Cochrane 2016).

## Danger Signs — When to Refer Immediately

Refer to hospital if any of the following:

1. Signs of severe dehydration (sunken eyes, very slow skin pinch, unconscious)
2. Bloody diarrhoea (dysentery — likely Shigella, needs antibiotics)
3. Vomiting repeatedly preventing ORT administration
4. High fever (> 38.5°C) in child under 3 months
5. No improvement after 3 hours of Plan B ORT
6. Unable to drink or breastfeed

## Cholera Cot Setup (Mass Casualty)

A cholera cot is a purpose-built stretcher with a central hole over a bucket
to collect stool and enable continuous measurement:

1. Foam mattress with waterproof cover; 10 cm hole at seat position
2. 20 L calibrated bucket below
3. ORS bag suspended on IV stand with wide-bore drinking tube
4. Record intake and output every 30 minutes
5. Replace stool volume with equal volume of ORS

Measurable intake-output balance is the key to preventing both under-treatment
(dehydration) and over-treatment (pulmonary oedema).

exercises.explanation:
Sunken eyes + thirsty (drinks eagerly) = 2 signs of 'some dehydration'. Plan B: 75 mL/kg x 15 kg = 1,125 mL over 4 hours = approximately 281 mL/hour. Re-assess after 4 hours.

Why the other options are wrong: Severe dehydration requires lethargic/unconscious + very sunken eyes + very slow (>2s) skin pinch. At 1.5s skin pinch and drinking eagerly, this is 'some' not 'severe' dehydration. Two clinical signs (sunken eyes, thirsty) confirm 'some dehydration' — Plan A is insufficient. Plan B ORS rehydration over 4 hours is needed. Plan B is 75 mL/kg over 4 hours. The 100 mL/kg over 6 hours is the IV regimen for Plan C in children under 5.

options.text: Some dehydration — Plan B: 75 mL/kg ORS over 4 hours = 1,125 mL
Severe dehydration — Plan C: IV Ringer's Lactate 100 mL/kg
No dehydration — Plan A: ORS after every loose stool only
Some dehydration — Plan B: 100 mL/kg over 6 hours

exercises.prompt: A 15 kg child has sunken eyes, is drinking eagerly, and skin pinch returns in 1.5 seconds. What WHO dehydration classification and treatment plan apply?

exercises.explanation: Home ORT: 6 level teaspoons sugar (30 g) + 0.5 teaspoon salt (2.5 g) per litre. Home ORT lacks potassium and bicarbonate found in WHO ORS sachets — it is a temporary measure only. Zinc: 10-14 days reduces episode duration by 25% and prevents future episodes for 2-3 months.
exercises.prompt: Home-made ORT uses 1 litre of clean water with ___ teaspoons of sugar and ___ teaspoon of salt. WHO recommends zinc supplementation for children under 5 for ___ days alongside ORT.

exercises.explanation: The WHO skin pinch test is key: immediate return = no dehydration; slow (<2s) = some; very slow (>2s) = severe. Two or more signs in a severity category are required for that classification.

left.text: Skin pinch returns in 3 seconds, patient unconscious

right.text: Severe dehydration

left.text: Child restless and irritable, eyes sunken, drinking eagerly

right.text: Some dehydration

left.text: Child well and alert, eyes normal, moist tongue

right.text: No dehydration

left.text: Very dry mouth, unable to drink, very sunken eyes

right.text: Severe dehydration

exercises.prompt: Match each dehydration sign to its severity category.

exercises.explanation:
Cholera toxin activates adenylate cyclase (cAMP), forcing Cl- secretion. However, the SGLT1 absorptive pathway is a completely separate mechanism — glucose carries Na+ across the enterocyte even during maximal secretion. ORT exploits this parallel absorption pathway.

Why the other options are wrong: There is no antitoxin in ORS. ORS does not neutralise cholera toxin. It works around the toxin by using a different absorptive pathway. ORS salt concentrations are far too low to be antibacterial. ORS replaces lost fluids and electrolytes — it does not treat the infection. ORS does not induce vomiting. It is given orally in small sips specifically to prevent vomiting. Vomiting is a danger sign requiring reassessment.

options.text: ORS neutralises the cholera toxin directly, stopping the secretory diarrhoea
Salt in ORS kills the Vibrio cholerae bacteria in the gut
Glucose activates the SGLT1 sodium-glucose co-transporter, which remains functional even when the secretory cAMP pump is active, allowing net sodium and water absorption
ORS induces vomiting of the toxin before it can cause secretion

exercises.prompt: Why does oral rehydration therapy work even when the cholera toxin is causing massive fluid secretion in the gut?

exercises.explanation: Untreated cholera CFR is 25-50% from dehydration alone. With ORT CFR drops below 1% — one of the most dramatic treatment effects in all of medicine. Plan B: 75 mL/kg x 25 kg = 1,875 mL over 4 hours.
exercises.prompt: Untreated cholera has a case fatality rate of ___%, which drops to below ___% with prompt oral rehydration therapy. A 25 kg child classified as Plan B needs ___ mL of ORS over 4 hours.

lessons.outline: Pathophysiology of secretory diarrhoea; WHO dehydration assessment (no dehydration, some dehydration, severe dehydration); WHO ORS formulation and home-made alternatives; ORT administration rates (Plan A, B, C); zinc supplementation evidence; BRAT/BRAF diet guidance; danger signs requiring IV fluids or hospital referral; cholera cot setup for mass casualty events.
lessons.title: Oral Rehydration Therapy & Diarrhoeal Disease

lessons.briefing: Malaria causes over 600,000 deaths per year, over 95% in sub-Saharan Africa, and over 80% in children under 5. Kenya has high malaria burden in lakeside, coastal, and western regions. A community health worker equipped with a rapid diagnostic test (RDT) and artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) can test, diagnose, and treat uncomplicated malaria at the household level — saving lives before referral is possible.
lessons.contentMd:
## Plasmodium Species in East Africa

| Species | Regional importance | Key features |
|---|---|---|
| P. falciparum | 99% of Kenya cases — most dangerous | Can infect all red blood cell ages; causes cerebral malaria |
| P. vivax | Occasional, mainly highland | Dormant liver stage (hypnozoite); relapses; requires primaquine |
| P. malariae | Rare | Long incubation (18-40 days); quartan fever (48-hr cycles) |
| P. ovale | Rare | Similar to vivax; relapsing |

**P. falciparum** is the primary target of all Kenya malaria control programmes.

## Anopheles Mosquito & Transmission

- Female Anopheles mosquitoes are the sole malaria vectors
- Biting behaviour: **peak biting time 2200h-0200h** (midnight hours)
- Preferred breeding sites: slow-moving or still water — rice paddies, hoofprints,
  irrigation channels, open water storage containers
- Sporogonic cycle in mosquito: 10-14 days at 25°C (pathogen develops in mosquito)
- Incubation in human after bite: 7-14 days for P. falciparum

## Clinical Presentation

### Uncomplicated Malaria (Classic Triad)

1. Fever (> 37.5°C), often with rigors (shaking chills)
2. Headache
3. Muscle pain and malaise

**Fever pattern by species:**
- P. falciparum: irregular (no classic pattern in early infection)
- P. vivax/ovale: tertian fever — spikes every 48 hours
- P. malariae: quartan fever — spikes every 72 hours

### Severe Malaria — Danger Signs (WHO)

Any ONE of the following = severe malaria → urgent referral:

1. Impaired consciousness / coma (cerebral malaria)
2. Multiple convulsions in 24 hours
3. Respiratory distress (acidotic breathing)
4. Circulatory collapse (systolic BP < 70 mmHg)
5. Jaundice + dark urine (blackwater fever — haemoglobinuria)
6. Abnormal bleeding
7. Severe anaemia (Hb < 5 g/dL)
8. Hypoglycaemia (blood glucose < 2.2 mmol/L)

## Rapid Diagnostic Tests (RDT)

Kenya National Malaria Programme recommends HRP2-based RDTs that detect
P. falciparum-specific histidine-rich protein 2.

### RDT Procedure

1. Clean fingertip with alcohol swab — allow to dry completely
2. Prick finger with sterile lancet — wipe away first drop
3. Collect 5 mcL blood with capillary tube
4. Transfer blood to sample well (S)
5. Add 2-3 drops of buffer solution
6. Read result at **15-20 minutes** (not before 15 min; not after 25 min)

### Reading the RDT

| Result | Lines visible | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| Negative | Control line (C) only | No P. falciparum antigen detected |
| Positive | Control (C) + Test line (T) | P. falciparum detected |
| Invalid | No control line appears | Test failed — repeat with new kit |

**Important**: Always treat on RDT result. A positive RDT = give ACT.
Do NOT treat a patient who tests RDT negative for malaria with ACT —
the fever has another cause.

## ACT Treatment — Artemether-Lumefantrine (AL)

Kenya first-line ACT: artemether-lumefantrine (Coartem, Lumartem)
Dosing by weight — 6-dose regimen over 3 days:

| Weight | Tablets per dose | Schedule |
|---|---|---|
| 5-14 kg (infants/young children) | 1 tablet | 0h, 8h, 24h, 36h, 48h, 60h |
| 15-24 kg (older children) | 2 tablets | same schedule |
| 25-34 kg (adolescents) | 3 tablets | same schedule |
| 35 kg and above (adults) | 4 tablets | same schedule |

**Key counselling points:**
- Give with food (fatty meal improves absorption by 3-fold — e.g. peanuts, milk, avocado)
- Complete all 6 doses even if fever resolves after dose 1-2
- Return immediately if vomits within 30 minutes of dose (repeat same dose)
- Return in 3 days for follow-up RDT

## Prevention — ITNs and IRS

**Insecticide-Treated Bed Nets (ITNs):**
- Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) retain efficacy for 3 years
- Hang net to cover entire sleeping area; tuck edges under mattress
- Effectiveness: 50% reduction in child malaria mortality
- Check for holes monthly; repair with needle and thread

**Indoor Residual Spraying (IRS):**
- Spray all internal walls and ceilings with approved insecticide
- Effective for 3-6 months per application cycle
- Move furniture away from walls before spraying
- Residents leave room for 30 minutes after spraying

exercises.explanation:
22 kg falls in the 15-24 kg weight band = 2 tablets per dose. The 6-dose regimen spans 3 days: 0h, 8h, then twice daily (24h, 36h, 48h, 60h). Fatty food increases AL absorption 3-fold.

Why the other options are wrong: 1 tablet is the dose for children 5-14 kg. At 22 kg the dose is 2 tablets per dose. 4 tablets is for adults 35 kg and above. Paediatric dosing is weight-banded. 22 kg = 2 tablets per dose, not a single adult dose. AL is a 6-dose 3-day regimen (not 5 days, not twice daily for the full period — doses are at 0h, 8h, 24h, 36h, 48h, 60h).

options.text: 2 tablets at 0h, 8h, 24h, 36h, 48h and 60h — give with food such as peanuts or milk
1 tablet at 0h, 8h, 24h, 36h, 48h and 60h
4 tablets in a single dose — adults and children over 15 kg take the same dose
2 tablets twice daily for 5 days

exercises.prompt: A 7-year-old child (22 kg) has a positive RDT and fever. What is the correct AL dosing regimen for this child?

exercises.explanation: Peak biting 2200h-0200h is why sleeping under an ITN during these hours is the primary protection. Incubation of 7-14 days means a returning traveller may not be symptomatic until 2 weeks after the infective bite — important for clinical history taking.
exercises.prompt: Female Anopheles mosquitoes peak biting time is between ___h and ___h. The incubation period for P. falciparum in the human after a bite is ___ to ___ days.

exercises.explanation: P. falciparum causes severe disease through multiple mechanisms acting simultaneously. Each danger sign reflects a different organ system failure and is an independent indication for urgent IV artesunate + referral.

right.text: Cerebral malaria — parasitised RBCs sequestered in brain capillaries
Blackwater fever — massive haemolysis releasing haemoglobin in urine
Destruction of red blood cells by parasite replication cycles
Parasite glucose consumption + impaired hepatic gluconeogenesis

exercises.prompt: Match each severe malaria danger sign to its physiological cause.

exercises.explanation:
The control line must always appear — its presence confirms the test ran correctly. No C line = invalid test regardless of T line status. Repeat with a new kit from a different lot if repeated invalids occur (possible storage problem).

Why the other options are wrong: No C line does not mean negative. It means the test failed. A valid negative shows C line only. Without C line the test gives no diagnostic information. A positive result shows C + T lines. No C line means invalid, regardless of whether T appears. The test has not functioned correctly. Kenya NMCP guidelines: treat only confirmed positives. Give empirical ACT only in high-transmission areas when RDT is unavailable. Repeat the test first.

options.text: The patient is negative for malaria — treat the fever as another cause
The patient is strongly positive — two lines always indicate severe infection
Give ACT immediately as a precaution since the result is unclear
The test is invalid — discard it and repeat with a new RDT kit

exercises.prompt: An RDT shows no line in the Control (C) position after 20 minutes. What should the community health worker do?

exercises.explanation: LLINs: factory-impregnated to last 3 years even with washing. 50% mortality reduction (RCT evidence, WHO malaria report 2023). AL vomiting: if < 30 minutes since ingestion, repeat the same dose (the tablet has not been absorbed). If > 30 minutes, do not repeat (assume absorbed even if some vomiting occurs).
exercises.prompt: Long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) retain efficacy for approximately ___ years and reduce child malaria mortality by approximately ___%. A patient who vomits AL within ___ minutes of a dose should receive the same dose again.

lessons.outline: Plasmodium species (falciparum, vivax, malariae, ovale); Anopheles mosquito lifecycle and biting behaviour; clinical presentation (uncomplicated vs severe malaria); rapid diagnostic tests (RDT) — HRP2 antigen basis, procedure, and reading results; artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) dosing by weight; artemether-lumefantrine (AL) 6-dose regimen; danger signs requiring referral; insecticide-treated bed nets (ITNs) and indoor residual spraying (IRS).

lessons.briefing: Vaccines are among the most cost-effective health interventions ever developed, but they are utterly dependent on a functioning cold chain. In East Africa's last-mile settings, a single power outage or broken refrigerator door seal can destroy an entire vaccine stock. Community health workers and vaccinators must master temperature monitoring, vaccine vial monitor (VVM) interpretation, and cold-box packing to protect every dose.
lessons.contentMd:
## Kenya EPI Schedule (Key Antigens)

| Age | Vaccines |
|---|---|
| Birth | OPV0, BCG, HepB birth dose |
| 6 weeks | OPV1, Pentavalent1 (DTP-HepB-Hib), PCV1, Rota1 |
| 10 weeks | OPV2, Pentavalent2, PCV2, Rota2 |
| 14 weeks | OPV3, Pentavalent3, PCV3, IPV |
| 6 months | Vitamin A (every 6 months to 5 years) |
| 9 months | Measles-Rubella (MR) 1st dose |
| 18 months | MR 2nd dose, Pentavalent booster |
| 9-14 years (girls) | HPV (2-dose schedule, 6 months apart) |

## Cold Chain Temperature Requirements

All vaccines must be stored at **+2°C to +8°C** at health facility level.

| Category | Temperature | Examples | Risk if wrong |
|---|---|---|---|
| Freeze-sensitive | +2 to +8°C — NEVER freeze | HepB, Pentavalent, HPV, PCV, Hib | Freezing destroys adjuvant aggregation; protein denaturation — no visible change |
| Freeze-tolerant | Can be briefly frozen | OPV, Rotavirus | Warmer end is bigger risk; freezing not ideal but less damaging |
| Heat-sensitive | +2 to +8°C | BCG, MR, Yellow Fever | Heat above 8°C denatures antigen; VVM provides early warning |

**Freeze-sensitive vaccines are the most common cause of vaccine failure** —
they show no visible change when frozen and then thawed, yet are completely
ineffective.

## Vaccine Vial Monitor (VVM)

A VVM is a small label on every vial containing a heat-sensitive chemical square.

| VVM Stage | Inner square vs outer ring | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Stage 1 (OK to use) | Inner square LIGHTER than outer ring | Use vaccine — good cold chain maintained |
| Stage 2 (OK to use) | Inner square SAME colour as outer ring | Use vaccine — but prioritise first (nearing end of life) |
| Stage 3 (DISCARD) | Inner square DARKER than outer ring | DO NOT USE — discard, report |
| Stage 4 (DISCARD) | Inner square completely DARK | DO NOT USE — discard, report |

**Rule:** Always check VVM before use. A Stage 1-2 VVM plus intact expiry date = safe to administer.

## Shake Test for Freeze Damage

For freeze-sensitive vaccines (Pentavalent, HepB, PCV, HPV):

1. Take one vial suspected of freezing and one known good control vial
2. Shake both vigorously for 10-15 seconds
3. Hold both up to light source
4. **Observe sedimentation at 30 minutes:**
   - Good control: slow, fine, uniform settling
   - Frozen vial: faster, larger, clumping sediment
5. If suspect vial settles faster/coarser than control → discard entire batch

## Cold Box and Vaccine Carrier Packing

### Cold Box (capacity: 4-48 hour field use)

1. Pre-cool cold box for 4 hours minimum with frozen icepacks inside
2. Line all walls with conditioned icepacks (conditioned = thawed to slushy/cool, NOT frozen — prevents freeze damage)
3. Pack vaccines in insulated bags in centre of box; never directly touching icepacks
4. Place temperature monitor (Fridge-tag or dial thermometer) in centre
5. Seal lid; do not open unnecessarily

### Conditioning Icepacks (Critical Step)

Conditioning prevents freeze-sensitive vaccines from contacting a surface
below 0°C:

1. Remove frozen icepacks from freezer
2. Leave at room temperature until water droplets form on surface (approximately 30-45 minutes)
3. Shake icepack — if you hear water sloshing, it is conditioned
4. Pack immediately into cold box

## Temperature Monitoring

| Tool | Frequency of reading | Action threshold |
|---|---|---|
| Electronic Fridge-tag | Continuous alarm | Alarm sounds if < 2°C or > 8°C; record and report |
| Dial thermometer | Twice daily (morning + afternoon) | If outside 2-8°C: move vaccines to alternate refrigerator |
| Manual log card | Each reading | Record date, time, temperature, initials; submit monthly |

Never ignore an alarm or an out-of-range reading. Report to vaccine focal person
within 2 hours and quarantine affected vaccines pending investigation.

## Open Vial Policy

| Vaccine | Open vial policy |
|---|---|
| OPV | Discard at end of each session day |
| MR | Discard at end of session (6 hours) |
| BCG | Discard 3 hours after opening |
| Pentavalent | Discard at end of session day |
| PCV | Discard at end of session day |

OPV is the only vaccine that can be returned to the cold chain after opening.
All others must be discarded once opened if not fully used in session.

## Vaccine Wastage Rate

Wastage Rate (%) = ((doses received - doses administered) / doses received) x 100

Target wastage rates (Kenya MOH):
- OPV: < 25%
- BCG: < 50% (single-dose vials are often multi-dose)
- Pentavalent/PCV: < 5%
- MR: < 10%

exercises.explanation:
VVM Stage 3 (inner darker than outer) = discard immediately. VVM indicates accumulated heat exposure that has likely compromised potency — expiry date only measures time, not heat. Both conditions must be met: VVM Stage 1-2 AND within expiry date.

Why the other options are wrong: Expiry date and VVM are independent checks. A VVM Stage 3 or 4 overrides a valid expiry date. The vaccine may have been heat-exposed and is potentially non-immunogenic. The shake test checks for freeze damage in freeze-sensitive vaccines. VVM Stage 3 indicates heat damage — a completely different issue. The answer is clear: discard. VVM Stage 3 is a discard instruction, not a prioritisation signal. Stage 2 (same colour) triggers prioritisation. Stage 3 (darker) = discard regardless.

options.text: Use the vial — the expiry date is still valid for 3 more months
Shake the vial to check for freeze damage before deciding
Discard the vial and report — VVM Stage 3/4 means heat damage regardless of expiry date
Use the vial first and prioritise it before newer stock

exercises.prompt: A health worker checks a Pentavalent vial and finds the inner VVM square is darker than the outer ring. The expiry date is still 3 months away. What should be done?

exercises.explanation: The 2-8°C range protects vaccines from both heat (above 8°C denatures antigens) and freeze damage (below 0°C destroys adjuvant in freeze-sensitive vaccines like Pentavalent). Conditioned icepacks (at 0°C, no longer deeply frozen) prevent direct contact with sub-zero surfaces.
exercises.prompt: Cold chain vaccines must be stored at ___ to ___ degrees C. Icepacks must be conditioned before packing with freeze-sensitive vaccines — conditioning is complete when ___ appear on the icepack surface and water sloshes inside.

exercises.explanation: BCG is particularly sensitive after reconstitution because the live attenuated bacteria are in suspension. MR is also a live attenuated vaccine with a 6-hour limit. OPV is uniquely allowed cold-chain return after opening.

right.text: 3 hours after reconstitution
End of session day (can be returned to cold chain)
End of session (within 6 hours of opening)
End of session day (do not return to cold chain)

exercises.explanation:
Overnight at 24°C is a cold chain breach. VVM Stage 1 means heat exposure hasn't yet shown on the indicator, but the shake test rules out freeze damage from condensation. The vaccine focal person reviews the event; the vials may still be usable if VVM is Stage 1-2 and the cold chain breach was brief.

Why the other options are wrong: VVM Stage 1 is necessary but not sufficient after a cold chain breach. The VVM measures cumulative heat — a single overnight event might not have moved the VVM yet but the vaccines must be quarantined pending investigation and decision by a qualified person. Automatic discard wastes potentially salvageable vaccines. The correct protocol is quarantine + shake test + reporting, not immediate discard without assessment. Simply returning to the refrigerator after a breach without documentation or assessment violates cold chain protocols. The breach must be documented and investigated.

options.text: Quarantine the vials and perform the shake test — if sedimentation passes, report to vaccine focal person who will decide based on full cold chain records
Use the vials immediately since VVM Stage 1 confirms they are good
Discard all 5 vials immediately without further investigation
Return them to the refrigerator — the VVM shows they are still safe

lessons.briefing: Early detection of disease outbreaks saves exponentially more lives than late response. Kenya's Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) system gives community health workers the tools to identify unusual illness clusters, trigger alerts within 24 hours, and implement initial containment while awaiting formal public health response. Speed and systematic recording are the two critical skills.
lessons.contentMd:
## Kenya IDSR — Priority Diseases

The Kenya Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response (IDSR) system categorises
diseases into three tiers based on response urgency:

### Tier 1 — Immediate (notify within 24 hours)

Any single case triggers immediate notification:

- Cholera, Ebola, Plague, Yellow Fever, Viral Haemorrhagic Fevers
- Polio (acute flaccid paralysis in a child under 15)
- Meningococcal disease (N. meningitidis confirmed)
- Unusual cluster of unexplained deaths

### Tier 2 — Weekly Reporting

- Malaria, TB, measles, typhoid, dysentery
- Notified weekly but investigated immediately if above threshold

### Alert Thresholds (Community Level)

An alert threshold triggers investigation even before confirmation:

- Cholera: any 1 case of acute watery diarrhoea in a person over 5 years
- Measles: any 1 case of fever + generalised rash
- Meningitis: any 2 cases of stiff neck + fever in same area within 1 week
- Unexplained deaths: 2+ deaths in same household within 48 hours

## Community-Level Detection

Community health workers are the **first sensor** in the surveillance system.
Key detection methods:

1. **Household register review**: monthly home visits reveal fever clusters
2. **Rumour surveillance**: gather information from community leaders, teachers,
   market traders about unusual illnesses
3. **Health facility crosscheck**: compare community report to facility attendance
4. **School absenteeism**: sudden cluster of absences may indicate outbreak

Detection formula — calculate attack rate by class or neighbourhood:
AR = cases / population x 100%

If AR in one cluster is > 3x the background rate, declare an alert.

## Case Definition

A standard case definition has three components:

| Component | Example (measles) |
|---|---|
| Clinical criteria | Fever AND generalised rash lasting 3+ days AND one of: cough, runny nose, or red eyes |
| Time criteria | Onset within the current reporting week |
| Place criteria | Resident in the affected sub-location |

**Suspected case**: meets clinical criteria only
**Probable case**: meets clinical + time + place criteria
**Confirmed case**: laboratory-confirmed (PCR, serology, culture)

Community action starts at suspected case level — do not wait for laboratory
confirmation to begin containment.

## Contact Tracing

A contact is anyone who has had close exposure to a confirmed case during
the infectious period:

| Disease | Infectious period | Quarantine period for contacts |
|---|---|---|
| Measles | 4 days before rash to 4 days after | 21 days from last exposure |
| Cholera | Duration of symptoms | Observe only; no quarantine if hygiene followed |
| Ebola | Onset of symptoms until recovery/death | 21 days from last exposure |
| Meningococcal | 7 days before symptoms | 10 days; chemoprophylaxis with ciprofloxacin |

### Contact Tracing Steps

1. Interview confirmed case: list all people contacted in last 2-21 days (disease-specific)
2. Visit each contact: take temperature, ask about symptoms, record in line list
3. Check daily for the full quarantine period
4. Escalate to clinic if contact develops fever or symptoms

## Isolation vs Quarantine

| Term | Who | Duration |
|---|---|---|
| Isolation | Confirmed or suspected CASE — infectious | Until no longer infectious |
| Quarantine | CONTACT — exposed but not yet ill | Incubation period of the disease |

A community isolation space should be:
- Separate room or building, not shared with family
- Good natural ventilation (cross-ventilation, open windows)
- Dedicated toilet/latrine not shared with rest of household
- Caregiver uses mask + hand hygiene when entering

## Line List Documentation

A line list records every case for rapid analysis:

| # | Name | Age | Sex | Village | Onset date | Symptoms | Outcome | Sample taken |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Patient A | 7 | F | Lwanda | 2026-10-01 | Fever, rash | Recovering | Yes |
| 2 | Patient B | 34 | M | Lwanda | 2026-10-03 | Fever, rash, cough | Active | Yes |

The line list enables calculation of: attack rate by age/sex/village; epidemic
curve (onset dates plotted over time); identification of common exposure source.

## Outbreak Communication — Messaging Without Panic

Effective community messaging during outbreaks:

1. **Acknowledge** the outbreak honestly; do not deny or minimise
2. **Explain** the disease in simple terms: what causes it, how it spreads
3. **Empower**: tell people what they can do (ORT, mosquito nets, handwashing)
4. **Direct**: give a clear action — "If you have fever and rash, go to [health post]"
5. **Consistent**: use the same message through community leaders, radio, and CHW visits
6. **Counter rumours**: proactively address false information; name the misinformation
   and replace it with evidence

Avoid: jargon, blame, stigmatising affected households, false reassurance.

exercises.explanation:
AR = 9/300 x 100 = 3%. For measles, the IDSR threshold is any 1 suspected case (fever + generalised rash) — immediate notification is required regardless of numbers. The cluster of 9 cases makes this urgent. Notify within 24 hours.

Why the other options are wrong: IDSR does not require laboratory confirmation before alerting. Suspected cases meeting clinical criteria trigger notification. Waiting for lab delays containment. AR = 9/300 x 100 = 3%, not 0.3%. The background rate of 0.5/100 = 0.5%. The village rate (3%) is 6x higher than background — clearly above threshold. Measles affects all unvaccinated ages. The IDSR threshold is any 1 suspected case — age restriction does not apply to triggering notification.

options.text: AR = 3%; no alert yet — wait for laboratory confirmation of at least 2 cases
AR = 0.3%; below the district background rate — monitor only
AR = 3%; trigger alert only if cases are in children under 5
AR = 3% (9/300 x 100); alert threshold exceeded — any single suspected measles case triggers immediate notification

exercises.prompt: In a village of 300 people, a community health worker identifies 9 cases of fever and rash in the same week, all within a 500-metre radius. The background measles rate in the district is 0.5 per 100 per week. What is the village attack rate, and should an alert be triggered?

exercises.explanation: Ebola maximum incubation is 21 days — contacts monitored for 21 days. Measles infectious period: 4 days before rash (late prodrome, highest viral shedding) to 4 days after rash appearance. This wide pre-rash infectious window is why measles spreads so rapidly before it is diagnosed.
exercises.prompt: An Ebola contact must be monitored for ___ days after last exposure. A measles case is infectious from ___ days before rash onset to ___ days after rash onset.

exercises.explanation: Alert thresholds are deliberately set low for high-consequence diseases. A single cholera case in a person over 5 is almost always epidemic cholera (El Tor) because sporadic cholera in adults is rare — any case requires immediate investigation of the water source.

right.text: Any 1 case of acute watery diarrhoea in a person over 5 years
Any 1 case of fever plus generalised rash
2 or more cases of stiff neck and fever in the same area within 1 week
2 or more deaths in the same household within 48 hours

exercises.explanation:
Isolation removes known or suspected infectious people from the community. Quarantine monitors exposed people who may or may not become ill — duration equals the disease's maximum incubation period. Both prevent forward transmission, but the target populations are different.

Why the other options are wrong: Isolation and quarantine are not categorised by disease severity. They are defined by whether the person IS infectious (isolation) or MIGHT BECOME infectious (quarantine). Both are public health measures, not medical prescriptions. Self-isolation and self-quarantine are both valid community-level approaches with CHW monitoring. Duration varies by disease. Ebola isolation lasts until recovery/death. Measles isolation ends 4 days after rash. Quarantine period = disease-specific maximum incubation.

options.text: Isolation separates confirmed or suspected infectious cases; quarantine separates exposed but not yet symptomatic contacts for the incubation period
Isolation is used for severe cases; quarantine is for mild cases
Quarantine requires a medical prescription; isolation can be self-managed
Isolation lasts 21 days for all diseases; quarantine lasts 14 days

exercises.explanation: Accurate, complete community health registers are the foundation of surveillance. A CHW who cannot maintain a register cannot detect unusual illness clusters early enough to trigger timely outbreak response.

Photograph the completed register page showing at least one household member's entry with: name, age, sex, village, date of last home visit, and any current health complaint.
